extracted.intended_audience: Christian clergy and informed laity (Protestant readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria for what counts as worship, idolatry, images, and related church practices; guidance on which rites and customs are scriptural or relics of paganism. Intended to judge acceptable corporate and private religious acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Worship (Cultus)
rubrics_metrics.description: To Pray to, to Swear by, to Obey, to bee Diligent, and Officious in Serving: in summe, all words and actions that betoken Fear to Offend, or Desire to Please, is Worship, whether those words and actions be sincere, or feigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worship is the outward signs and actions that indicate inward honor; these outward signs (words, gestures, ceremonies) are called cultus in Latin and are ordinarily equivalent to honour. The internal intention differentiates the moral quality of worship but outward acts are the usual indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Divine and Civil Worship
rubrics_metrics.description: The Worship we exhibite to those we esteem to be but men ... is Civill Worship: But the worship we exhibite to that which we think to bee God, whatsoever the words, ceremonies, gestures, or other actions be, is Divine Worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts like prostration before a king are civil worship if the person is acknowledged as a mortal; removing a hat in a church may be divine worship if understood as honouring God. Terms douleia and latreia (Greek) distinguish slave-service from general service but do not map neatly to divine vs civil — one must judge by the intention and attribution of infinite power.

rubrics_metrics.name: What an Image Is
rubrics_metrics.description: An IMAGE (in the most strict signification of the word) is the Resemblance of some thing visible... the Phantasticall Formes, Apparitions, or Seemings of Visible Bodies to the Sight ... are onely Images; such as ... Reflexion, or Refraction ... and are present oftentimes in our Imagination, and in our Dreams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images properly denote visible resemblances or mental phantasms (ideas/idols). There can be no true image of God or any infinite thing; only of visible bodies. Material images may represent a maker's phantasm rather than the original object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idolatry defined
rubrics_metrics.description: To worship an Image, is voluntarily to doe those externall acts, which are signes of honoring either the matter of the Image ... or the Phantasme of the brain, for the resemblance, or representation whereof, the matter was formed and figured; or both together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idolatry occurs when finite things (stone, wood, images, or phantasms) are honoured as if they were divine or as if they heard prayers or saw devotions. Praying to an image for things only God can give, or believing an image has divine power, is idolatry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scandalous (Seeming) Worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Scandalous Worship ... is but Seeming Worship; and may sometimes bee joined with an inward, and hearty detestation ... and proceed onely from the fear of death, or other grievous punishment; and is neverthelesse a sin in them that so worship, in case they be men whose actions are looked at by others, as lights to guide them by.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External compliance under compulsion is not necessarily idolatry for the compelled individual, but when done by pastors or influential persons without clear disavowal it gives scandal and causes others to err. The culpability depends on the actor's role and the likelihood their action will be imitated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worship in a dedicated place or toward an image not automatically idolatry
rubrics_metrics.description: To worship God, in some peculiar Place, or turning a mans face towards an Image, or determinate Place, is not to worship, or honor the Place, or Image; but to acknowledge it Holy ... which implies no new quality in the Place, or Image; but onely a new Relation by Appropriation to God; and therefore, is not Idolatry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a place or an image as an aid to worship (a memorial, a dedication authorized by God or legitimate church authority) is permissible if the worship is directed to God and not to the place or image as containing divine substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributing divine presence to finite place or image is idolatry
rubrics_metrics.description: To worship God, is inanimating, or inhibiting, such Image, or place; that is to say, an infinite substance in a finite place, is Idolatry: for such finite Gods, are but Idols of the brain, nothing reall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one treats an image or place as actually containing God (an 'infinite substance' in a finite thing) rather than as a sign or memorial, that crosses into idolatry. The key test is whether one ascribes independent divine power or presence to the object.

rubrics_metrics.name: God‑appointed images are not precedents for human-instituted worship
rubrics_metrics.description: The places of Scripture pretended to countenance the setting up of Images ... As for the proofs alledged out of Scripture, namely, those examples of Images appointed by God to bee set up; They were not set up for the people, or any man to worship; but that they should worship God himselfe before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples such as the Cherubim over the Ark or the Brazen Serpent were set by divine command and were meant as places to worship God before, not objects to be worshipped; copying such examples as grounds for making images to be worshipped is invalid. Hezekiah's destruction of the brazen serpent (because people worshipped it) is cited as precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting visions or phantasms is not sinful, worshipping them is
rubrics_metrics.description: I say not, that to draw a Picture after a fancy, is a Sin; but when it is drawn, to hold it for a Representation of God, is against the second Commandement; and can be of no use, but to worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic depiction of visions, angels, or saints is allowed as representation or monument; the sin arises when such depictions are regarded as literal representations of divine reality and are worshipped as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonizing Saints is a relic of paganism (unauthorized by Scripture)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Canonizing of Saints, is another Relique of Gentilisme ... The first that ever was canonized at Rome, was Romulus ... And thereupon the Senate gave Publique Testimony of his Sanctity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal canonization resembles Roman apotheosis and is presented as a human institution not grounded in Scripture; therefore canonization as practiced is criticized as a pagan relic, not a scriptural requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal title and authority derived from Roman civil tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Name Of Pontifex ... This was the name of him that in the ancient Common-wealth of Rome, had the Supreme Authority ... From whence wee may by the way observe, that there is no place for the superiority of the Pope over other Bishops, except in the territories whereof he is himself the Civill Soveraign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pope's claim to universal ecclesiastical supremacy is historically rooted in Roman civil office and imperial endorsement; practical and legitimate ecclesiastical superiority exists only where the pope is also the civil sovereign or where civil authority has explicitly invested him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processions, candles, torches and other ceremonies as pagan relics
rubrics_metrics.description: The carrying about of Images in Procession, ... To these Processions also belonged the bearing of burning Torches, and Candles, before the Images of the Gods ... And in processe of time, the devout, but ignorant People, did many times honor their Bishops with the like pompe of Wax Candles, and the Images of our Saviour, and the Saints, constantly, in the Church it self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ceremonial elements (processions, wax candles, torches, holy water, festivals) have parallels in pagan rites and are characterized as relics inherited from Gentile religions; their presence in Christian practice is to be judged by whether they lead to idolatry or scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exorcism and extraordinary gifts are not normative for all believers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Power Of Casting Out Devills, Not The Same It Was In The Primitive Church ... those extraordinary gifts were given to the Church, for no longer a time, than men trusted wholly to Christ ... and consequently ... these supernaturall gifts of God were again taken from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miraculous signs (casting out devils, speaking with new tongues, immunity to poison) were temporary dispensations for a particular stage of the Church; absence of such gifts now is not a sign of deficiency in faith, and ordinary Christians should not assume universal entitlement to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between worship out of fear under compulsion and voluntary worship
rubrics_metrics.description: To worship God, ... if hee that doth it, should suppose the Soule of the Prince to be in the Stool, or should present a Petition to the Stool, it were Divine Worship, and Idolatry ... But if hee that doth it, be compelled by terrour of Death, or other great corporall punishment, it is not Idolatry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions performed under coercion (fear of death or punishment) do not necessarily signify inward honour and therefore may not amount to idolatry. However, when performed by those whose example instructs others, failure to manifest disapproval publicly can become scandalous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of images as monuments or civil honour is permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: I say not, that to draw a Picture after a fancy, is a Sin ... And the same may be said of the Images of Angels, and of men dead; unlesse as Monuments of friends, or of men worthy remembrance: For such use of an Image, is not Worshyp of the Image; but a civill honoring of the Person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material images may be tolerated as commemorative monuments or for civil honour (e.g., memorials of the dead) provided they are not treated as objects of divine worship or thought to possess supernatural powers.
